newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazilian govt hopeful re-election bill will pass.
newsitem.headline: Brazilian govt hopeful re-election bill will pass.

text.p: The Brazilian government is increasingly confident it will have its way this week when it puts a bill allowing re-election of sitting presidents to a vote in Congress, newspapers reported on Sunday.

President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, whose dream of being Brazil's first re-elected leader has been stumbling through a minefield of vested interests and opposition, persuaded a powerful foe to join his fold, the Jornal do Brasil daily said.

The paper said that after secret talks Friday night with Cardoso, ex-president and current head of the Senate Jose Sarney said "re-election would pass", a significant concession from one of the bill's most ardent critics.
Fearful of the legacy of past imperial powers, Brazil has never allowed sitting presidents, governors or mayors to seek a second consecutive term.

Cardoso, midway through his four-year reign, has recently made a constitutional amendment allowing re-election the flagship reform of his administration, arguing that economic stability required political continuity.
Putting a gun to the heads of opponents within its own ranks, the government is insisting on a lower house vote on the bill Wednesday.

For that, it needs the votes of the largest party in Congress, Sarney's Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB), which two weeks ago decided not to vote on re-election until after elections for the presidencies of the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate in early February.

The Folha de Sao Paulo newspaper reported heavy lobbying by government leaders had in the past week won 28 more deputies to their side, giving Cardoso 320 certain votes in favor of re- election in the lower house when only 308 were necessary.
"This allows the government to bet everything on January 29 (the date of the vote)," Folha said.
Last week, Cardoso threatened to banish the PMDB from the government if it continued to hamper his bid for re-election.

On Sunday, some newspapers wrote scorching articles accusing senior PMDB figures of opposing re-election for purely personal reasons, such as not wanting to have to run against Cardoso in the next presidential elections in 1998.
The Correio Braziliense newspaper published a survey showing a record 66 percent approval rating for the president in the Federal District of Brasilia.

"Behind all the speeches in favor or against re-election, there lurk personal interests," it wrote, adding that no one with serious presidential aspirations would want to run against someone as popular as Cardoso currently is.
Tongue in cheek, the Estado de Sao Paulo newspaper noted that the battle for votes in Congress had adversely affected the health of deputies and senators.
"An agitated week of lunches and dinners in Brasilia has put an end to the diets of everyone in Congress, provoking indigestion all around," it wrote.
